title: Stone Does Not Vote
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The councilor smiled at Toph as if he'd already decided what she would say.

"Master Beifong," he began, "surely with your abilities you can tell us which section of the new bridge is unsafe."

Toph folded her arms.

"I can tell you which part is cracked."

"Excellent. Then we'll take your word as our final finding."

"No."

The room went still.

It was a council session held at Lanternwell Square, open to the public because the bridge connected several districts and affected more than one neighborhood's budget. We sat on simple benches beneath the old lantern hooks. On the wall hung Aang's revised survey and a map showing the garden at Riverstone Terrace.

The councilor, whose name was Daron, looked momentarily confused.

"Is the damage unclear?"

"The damage is clear. Your question is wrong."

Daron adjusted his collar.

"I beg your pardon?"

Toph put both feet flat against the stone floor.

"You want me to listen to the rock and announce a perfect answer so nobody has to ask the people who use the bridge. Stone doesn't know which carts are too wide, who needs a handrail, or how far a person can walk carrying water."

Daron glanced toward Aang.

I recognized the look. Somebody asking the most famous person in the room to translate a woman who had spoken perfectly clearly.

Aang folded his hands.

"I think Toph explained it well."

I tried not to smile.

Daron turned back to her.

"But your earth sense is the strongest evidence available."

"It's one kind of evidence."

"Surely it should take precedence."

Toph's smile was sharp.

"Surely you should sit down before you embarrass yourself further."

"Toph," I murmured.

"What? That was polite."

The chairwoman tapped her bell.

We had invited Fen, Danse, Sela, two cart drivers, and Edda, who used a wheeled chair for longer distances and had asked to speak about the bridge approach. The council had assumed they were there to observe. The assumption lasted only until Edda rose to her hands.

"I'd like the floor," she said.

The chairwoman looked at Daron, then nodded.

Edda moved to the front with practiced patience. The table had been set too close to a bench, and someone had to shift it before she could approach.

"That's my first point," she said when the path was clear. "You built a meeting room with an obstacle in the middle. Then you're going to tell me how convenient the bridge is."

A few people laughed nervously.

Edda did not.

"The handrail is too high on the north end. The ramp angle changes where the path was patched. When the stone is wet, my wheels lose traction. Master Beifong's assessment of the foundations is useful. It doesn't tell you any of that."

Toph nodded.

"Exactly."

Daron looked at his notes as though they had personally betrayed him.

Danse stepped forward with the pressure tests from Brasswatch. He had calculated how much weight the bridge could carry under several conditions. Tamsin added a list of materials and repair hours. Fen explained how a closed bridge changed the delivery routes.

Sela spoke last.

"The drainage problem you're discussing isn't just about the bridge," she said. "Your cart path blocks the spillway into my garden. If you redirect that water without speaking to us, you may save the bridge and flood our home."

Aang looked down at the map.

He didn't defend the old decision. He wrote the new information beside the survey.

I felt something loosen in my chest.

That was what I wanted a council to look like: not a room full of people performing certainty, but one willing to admit what had been missed.

A clerk at the end of the bench unfolded a second map that had not been included in the council packet. It showed the route used by the water carriers when the canal rose, with a narrow detour marked in charcoal.

"Why wasn't this with the first survey?" I asked.

The clerk looked toward Daron. "It was submitted after the deadline."

"The water doesn't read your deadlines," Toph said.

Daron's jaw tightened. I thought he might defend the rule. Instead he asked the clerk to date the late submission and make it part of the public record.

Sela came forward to check whether her garden had been marked correctly. Beren pointed out that the detour was narrow enough to turn a handcart but not a loaded wagon. Toph knelt and pressed her palm against the paving stones; she could tell them where the foundations had shifted, but she did not pretend to know what a wagon could do.

Aang asked the carrier to explain the route without interpreting it for them. Katara wanted to know how water and medicine would reach the clinic if the bridge stayed closed during another storm.

For once I did not have to fill the room with a speech about listening. The people who crossed the bridge were doing the work of being heard. Daron wrote the new questions on the agenda, scratching out the words FINAL FINDING. The small noise of his pen against paper sounded more useful than another grand declaration of unity.

Daron, to his credit, listened. After a long silence he put down his pencil.

"I've been treating Master Beifong's evidence as a way to settle the matter quickly."

Toph lifted her chin.

"Yes."

"That was unfair to the other witnesses."

"Also yes."

He swallowed.

"And to you."

She considered him.

"Better."

The chairwoman proposed a working group with specific responsibilities. Toph would assess structural movement. Edda and other bridge users would test access and safety. Danse and Tamsin would handle materials and loads. Sela and the gardeners would review drainage consequences. Fen would update the delivery plans.

Nobody would be expected to answer questions outside their expertise, and the bridge would remain closed until the work was safe.

It wasn't a romantic decision. It was slower, more expensive, and likely to irritate half the people in the square.

It was right.

After the meeting, Toph marched away before anyone could congratulate her. I caught up with her beside the fountain.

"You were brilliant," I said.

She scowled.

"Don't."

"Why?"

"Because everybody says that when I break a rock. It gets old."

"You didn't break anything."

"Exactly."

I walked beside her in silence. Her boots made soft sounds on the paving stones. She stopped near the canal.

"I wanted to," she admitted.

"Break something?"

"Make a demonstration. Show him what I could do. I could've split the bad section out of the bridge in one motion and made the whole room stare."

"But?"

"But the kid who brings water across it wouldn't get home any faster."

I touched her hand.

"That's what impressed me."

She turned her face away.

"Gross."

"You're welcome."

We sat on the low wall, close enough that our shoulders touched. Toph rested her fingers against the stone, feeling the vibrations from carts crossing the safer street beyond the canal.

"I hate when people turn me into a tool," she said.

"I know."

"They think being good at something means they own the answer."

"That happens to Maui too. And Danse. And Aang."

"Yeah. Only I'm right more often."

I laughed.

She smiled despite herself.

Toph rested her palm against the wall. The stone carried footsteps from the market street, uneven and familiar. I waited for her to speak.

"There's a crack in the approach nobody mentioned," she said.

"Should we go back?"

"Tomorrow. With the actual inspection crew. If I march in there now, everybody'll think I've solved it by touching a rock."

She sounded angry, but there was amusement underneath it too. I had learned not to mistake her confidence for an endless supply of patience.

"Do you think they'll listen when you bring it up?"

"Maybe. They listened today when I told them a rock doesn't vote."

"Very eloquent."

"I should put it on a banner."

I laughed.

She took a breath. "Sometimes I want to show them what I can do. Really show them. Make the whole bridge bend until nobody can pretend they know more about stone than me."

"That sounds satisfying."

"It would be. For ten seconds. Then somebody's garden floods because I moved the wrong support."

I reached for her hand but stopped where she could feel me coming. She caught my fingers herself.

"You're allowed to be good at things without being assigned every problem," I said.

"Yeah. You keep saying that."

"Because you keep forgetting."

She turned toward me, the edge of a smile on her face. "Careful, Sparky. I might start believing you."

We agreed to bring the crack to the paid inspection team, not to make a spectacle of it. Sela would be invited to comment before any drainage work touched her garden. Edda would review the temporary walking route. Toph wanted the findings written down in the ordinary record, not recorded as another miracle performed by a famous bender.

I told her how proud I was of that.

"Don't get sentimental," she said.

"Too late."

She leaned closer, paused and waited until I answered with a small movement of my own. The kiss was brief and warm. When we drew apart she pretended the canal breeze had made her blush.

"We're still getting dumplings," she said.

"After the inspection tomorrow?"

"Before. I'm not negotiating on an empty stomach."

I laughed, and she squeezed my hand. When the messenger arrived a few minutes later with Katara's letter, there was still a little flour on Toph's sleeve from the dumpling stall. It made the ordinary details of our life feel as important as anything the council had written down.

A messenger approached with a small packet from the South. It was Katara's handwriting on the envelope. We opened it together because she'd addressed it to the household.

The clinic was busy. The new treatment room was functioning. She'd heard about the bridge meeting from a traveler and wanted to know whether Toph had frightened the council into competence.

Toph grinned.

"Tell her yes."

I read the rest of the letter. Katara asked about our schedules, the repair budget, and whether we were eating properly. In the margin she had drawn a small bowl with four chopsticks.

"She misses us," I said.

"Obviously."

Toph's voice softened.

"I miss her too."

We wrote back at the kitchen table that evening. Aang described the aerial survey. I added the council decision and the new working group. Toph dictated a paragraph about how she'd managed not to throw anybody into the canal, which she considered a tremendous personal sacrifice.

When the ink dried, we ate dinner by the open window.

Afterward Toph found me alone in the garden.

"Hey, Jasper."

"Hey."

She stood near the gate, her hands in her pockets.

"You know that Friday space on the calendar?"

I felt a smile start.

"Yes."

"I've decided."

"Oh?"

"I want it."

I moved closer.

"All right."

"Not because I owe you a date."

"I know."

"And not because you were nice to me today."

"I know."

She reached for my hand, found it without hesitation, and tugged me toward her.

"Because I like you, idiot."

I laughed into the kiss. She kissed me again, softer this time, and for a moment the whole complicated house with its unfinished repairs and missing chair felt like exactly where I wanted to be.

On Friday we walked to the bridge together and checked the new ramp markings.

The bridge was still closed.

Toph tapped the stone beneath her feet.

"Still talking," she said.

"What's it saying?"

"That we've got work to do."

She grinned.

I squeezed her hand.

For once, neither of us was in a hurry to prove otherwise.
